content: Due to the potential for both induction and inhibition of the CYP2B6 enzyme when cannabidiol is co-administered with CYP2B6 substrates, it may be clinically appropriate to consider reducing the dosage of the CYP2B6 substrates. Rifampin decreases carvedilol levels or effects by enhancing its metabolism through the hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10. This interaction necessitates caution and monitoring. Similarly, rifampin reduces caspofungin levels by increasing its metabolism, requiring careful monitoring. Cenobamate decreases rifampin levels or effects by affecting CYP2B6 metabolism. Therapy adjustments and close monitoring are recommended, including increasing the dose of CYP2B6 substrates as needed when co-administered with cenobamate. Rifampin also reduces cevimeline levels or effects by influencing CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Additionally, rifampin decreases the levels or effects of chlordiazepoxide, chloroquine, and citalopram by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring similar caution and monitoring. Rifampin increases the toxicity of cholic acid by reducing its elimination. Concomitant use of bile salt efflux pump (BSEP) inhibitors should be avoided, as this may exacerbate the accumulation of conjugated bile salts in the liver, potentially leading to clinical symptoms. If co-administration is necessary, serum transaminases and bilirubin levels should be monitored. Rifampin also reduces the levels or effects of clarithromycin, clomipramine, clonazepam, and clorazepate by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Clotrimazole increases rifampin levels or effects through an unspecified mechanism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Co-administration with cotrimoxazole increases rifampin concentrations, potentially raising the risk of toxicity, so adverse reactions should be monitored. Rifampin reduces clozapine levels or effects by affecting CYP1A2 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin decreases the levels or effects of conjugated estrogens (oral and vaginal) and cortisone by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. This interaction requires caution and monitoring. Rifampin also reduces crizotinib levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, while crizotinib increases rifampin levels via P-glycoprotein, necessitating caution and monitoring. Rifampin decreases cyclophosphamide levels or effects by affecting CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy adjustments and monitoring are recommended. Similarly, rifampin reduces cyclosporine levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transporters, requiring close monitoring and therapy modification. Danicopan increases rifampin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein transporters, necessitating caution and monitoring. Rifampin reduces dantrolene levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring similar caution. Rifampin also decreases daprodustat levels or effects, likely through CYP2C8 induction, which may result in reduced efficacy. Hemoglobin levels and daprodustat doses should be monitored and adjusted as needed. Rifampin reduces dapsone levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Similarly, rifampin decreases daunorubicin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein transporters, necessitating monitoring. Rifampin also reduces deferasirox levels, and concomitant use of potent UGT inducers should be avoided. If co-administration is required, the initial dose of deferasirox should be increased to 30 mg/kg, with ferritin levels and clinical response monitored. Rifampin decreases deflazacort and dexamethasone levels or effects by affecting P-glycoprotein transporters, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin also reduces dexlansoprazole levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism, necessitating caution. Similarly, rifampin decreases diazepam levels or effects (both buccal and intranasal formulations) by affecting CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin reduces digoxin levels or effects by increasing its metabolism and affecting P-glycoprotein transporters, necessitating caution and monitoring. Rifampin also decreases disopyramide and docetaxel levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transporters, requiring similar caution. Rifampin reduces dolutegravir levels or effects by increasing its metabolism. Therapy adjustments, including increasing dolutegravir dosage, are recommended when co-administering with strong UGT1A/CYP3A4 inducers. An alternative to rifampin should be considered in patients with integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI)-associated resistance, as concomitant use may result in therapeutic failure and resistance development. Rifampin decreases donepezil, doxepin, and doxorubicin levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transporters, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin also reduces dronabinol levels or effects by affecting CYP2C9/10 and CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating similar caution. Rifampin decreases dutasteride and duvelisib levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transporters, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin also reduces efavirenz levels or effects by affecting CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 metabolism, necessitating caution. Rifampin decreases elafibranor levels or effects by increasing its metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin also affects elagolix levels, increasing its effects via P-glycoprotein transporters while decreasing its levels through CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy adjustments and monitoring are recommended, with a 6-month limit on concomitant use of elagolix 150 mg daily and rifampin. Rifampin reduces eltrombopag levels or effects by affecting CYP1A2 and CYP2C9/10 metabolism, while eltrombopag increases rifampin levels by decreasing its metabolism. This interaction requires caution and monitoring.
